rationale: A wins because it understands the proof burden and keeps the founder away from easy overclaims. Its line, "A single average with no distribution behind it will not survive a data reporter's first question," is exactly the adult supervision this story needs. B has real material, especially "The Enterprise AI Agent That Insists Humans Stay in the Loop," but then it wanders into "payment-level visibility into $80B" and a competitive moat the update does not actually prove. That's not strategy; that's a slide deck trying on a trench coat.
gaps_in_A: "Ramp's new agent cancels your software subscriptions" overstates the autonomy. The update says the agent drafts cancellation or renegotiation emails that finance approves.
"SaaS pricing has depended on customers not auditing their own seat counts closely" is a broad industry motive claim. Plausible, but not grounded in the supplied facts.
"The first AI agents in finance departments aren't doing the math" reaches past the evidence. The update supports this Ramp workflow, not a first-wave category claim.

"charging for the approval workflow" assumes the enterprise tier is paid and monetized around approvals. The update only says an enterprise tier with custom approval workflows is coming later this year.
gaps_in_B: "Ramp's payment-level visibility into $80B in annualized volume gives it transaction-native intelligence" is the big foul. The update says Ramp processes purchase volume and the agent scans spend; it does not prove payment-level data architecture or a moat.

"Companies Are Wasting an Average of $342,000 a Year on Software They Don't Use" flattens the fact. The update says savings came mostly from unused seats and auto-renewals, not simply software nobody uses.
"drawn from 200 real customers" upgrades "200-company beta" into customers. That may be true, but it is not in the provided facts.
"SaaS vendors profit structurally from auto-renewals and shelfware" is a loaded market claim. It needs vendor economics evidence, not just Ramp beta savings.
